subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Resources and Economics Readings
subtitle: Reading passages and comprehension questions about resource geography and economic choices.
description: Five reading passages with questions on resources, economic sectors, trade, case studies, sustainability, and misconceptions.

data.sourcePassage: A material becomes a resource when people can use it and value it. Oil became extremely valuable after engines, factories, cars, ships, and aeroplanes needed fuel. Wind has always existed, but modern turbines allow people to turn it into electricity. Lithium became more important as rechargeable batteries became common in phones, laptops, and electric vehicles. Resources are not spread evenly across Earth. Geology, climate, landforms, water availability, soil, and technology all affect where resources are found and how people use them. Because no region has everything it needs, places often trade resources they have for resources they lack.

questions.question: According to the passage, when does a material become a resource?
options: When people can use it and value it
When it is impossible to trade
When it has no economic use
questions.modelAnswer: A material becomes a resource when people can use it and value it.

questions.question: Which factor helps explain where minerals and fossil fuels are found?
questions.modelAnswer: Geology helps explain where minerals and fossil fuels form.

questions.question: Explain why technology can change whether something is useful as a resource.
questions.modelAnswer: Technology can make resources easier to find, extract, process, or use. Wind became more useful for electricity when turbines improved, and lithium became more important when rechargeable batteries became common.

questions.question: Why does uneven resource distribution encourage trade?
questions.modelAnswer: Uneven distribution means places have different resources. They often export resources they have in large amounts and import resources they lack.

questions.question: Give one example of how a resource can become more or less valuable over time.
questions.modelAnswer: Lithium became more valuable as phones, laptops, and electric vehicles needed rechargeable batteries. Oil became more valuable after fuel-powered transport and industry expanded.

data.sourcePassage: Economic activity is often divided into sectors. The primary sector collects raw materials from nature, such as farming, fishing, forestry, and mining. The secondary sector turns raw materials into products through factories, construction, or food processing. The tertiary sector provides services such as health care, transportation, education, and retail. The quaternary sector is linked to knowledge, research, data, and technology. People often settle near resources because resources can provide food, water, jobs, trade routes, building materials, energy, and transport access. However, resource-based settlement can be risky. A mining town may shrink if a mine closes, and a farming community may struggle during drought.

questions.question: Which economic sector collects raw materials from nature?
questions.modelAnswer: The primary sector collects raw materials from nature.

questions.question: Which activity belongs in the secondary sector?
questions.modelAnswer: Food processing belongs in the secondary sector because it turns raw materials into products.

questions.question: Why have people often settled near rivers, fertile soil, forests, coalfields, or harbours?
questions.modelAnswer: These places can provide food, water, jobs, building materials, trade routes, energy, and transport access.

questions.question: Explain one risk of a settlement depending on a single resource.
questions.modelAnswer: If the resource runs out, prices fall, a mine closes, or drought affects farming, jobs and income may decline and people may move away.

questions.question: How might a region change as it moves from primary work to quaternary work?
questions.modelAnswer: It may shift from extracting resources to using education, technology, research, internet access, universities, and data jobs. Infrastructure and skills become especially important.

data.sourcePassage: No region has everything it needs. Interdependence means places depend on each other for resources, goods, services, labour, and markets. A country may import oil but export wheat. A city may import food from rural farms and export services such as banking, education, or technology. A factory may use parts from several countries to make one product. Trade can bring more choices, jobs, access to resources, and economic growth. It can also create challenges, including dependence on distant suppliers, pollution from transportation, unequal profits, and vulnerability during wars, disasters, strikes, or supply chain delays. A supply chain shows the path from raw material to final use, waste, or recycling.

questions.question: What does interdependence mean in the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Interdependence means places depend on each other.

questions.question: Which is listed as a challenge of trade?
questions.modelAnswer: Dependence on distant suppliers is a challenge of trade.

questions.question: Explain how a laptop supply chain can connect several places.
questions.modelAnswer: Minerals may be mined in one country, parts made in several countries, assembly done elsewhere, and design, software, shipping, and sales spread across many regions.

questions.question: Why can a disaster in one place affect products far away?
questions.modelAnswer: Global supply chains link distant places, so a flood, war, port closure, fuel shortage, or factory shutdown can delay materials and products elsewhere.

questions.question: Why should geographers ask who earns profit and who faces environmental impacts in a supply chain?
questions.modelAnswer: Those questions reveal whether benefits and costs are shared fairly. Some places may gain profit while others experience pollution, low wages, or resource damage.

data.sourceTitle: Case Studies: Oil, Farming, Minerals, Tourism, and Water
data.targetTitle: Case Studies: Oil, Farming, Minerals, Tourism, and Water
data.sourcePassage: The source describes several resource-based case studies. Oil in the Middle East can bring export income, energy jobs, infrastructure, and services, but economies may depend too heavily on one resource and oil prices can rise and fall. Agriculture in the US Great Plains benefits from broad open land, fertile soils, railways, and highways, but drought, irrigation pressure, soil erosion, and changing markets create challenges. Rare earth minerals support smartphones, electric vehicles, wind turbines, and defence equipment, yet mining and processing can damage land and water if poorly managed. Caribbean tourism uses beaches, warm climate, coral reefs, music, food, and culture to create jobs, but hurricanes, seasonal work, expensive imports, and reef damage are risks. In the American Southwest, low rainfall, high evaporation, growing cities, irrigated farming, and shared rivers make water management both environmental and economic.

questions.question: Which region is linked to large oil reserves in the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: The Middle East is linked to large oil reserves.

questions.question: Which case study is most closely linked to cattle, wheat, corn, and soybeans?
questions.modelAnswer: US Great Plains agriculture is most closely linked to those products.

questions.question: Why might an oil-rich country still want to develop tourism, finance, renewable energy, or technology?
questions.modelAnswer: It may want to diversify so the economy is less dependent on one resource and less vulnerable to price changes or future decline.

questions.question: Explain why clean energy technology still requires careful resource planning.
questions.modelAnswer: Clean energy equipment can require minerals such as rare earths. Mining and processing them can damage land and water, and supply chains may depend on a few suppliers.

questions.question: How are water scarcity in the Southwest and tourism in the Caribbean both examples of human-environment interaction?
questions.modelAnswer: In both cases, people use environmental features for economic activity, but the environment also creates limits and risks such as drought, storms, reef damage, and water pressure.

data.sourcePassage: Sustainability is about meeting present needs while protecting the ability of future generations to meet theirs. It is not only about nature; it also includes people, fairness, and long-term economic planning. Sustainable resource decisions ask whether workers and communities are treated fairly, whether pollution is reduced, whether ecosystems are protected, and whether the economy can stay stable over time. Common misconceptions can lead to weak geography answers. Renewable resources are not unlimited, because forests, fish, soil, and freshwater can be damaged or used too quickly. High population does not always mean high population density, because density depends on people per unit of area. Economic growth can create jobs and income, but benefits may be uneven and some communities may face pollution, displacement, high housing costs, or low wages.

questions.question: What does sustainability protect besides present needs?
questions.modelAnswer: Sustainability protects future needs as well as present needs.

questions.question: Which statement corrects a misconception from the passage?
options: Renewable resources still need careful management
Renewable resources can never be damaged
Economic growth always helps everyone equally
questions.modelAnswer: Renewable resources still need careful management.

questions.question: Explain why sustainability includes both environmental and economic thinking.
questions.modelAnswer: People need resources for jobs and daily life, but overuse or pollution can harm ecosystems and future opportunities. Sustainable choices balance needs, fairness, and long-term stability.

questions.question: Why is it misleading to say that a high population always means a place is crowded?
questions.modelAnswer: Crowding depends on population density. A place can have many people but a large land area, so people may not live close together everywhere.

questions.question: Why should a town considering a new mine include many stakeholders in the decision?
questions.modelAnswer: Different stakeholders may experience different benefits and risks. Workers, families, Indigenous communities, farmers, scientists, government, and businesses can provide evidence and perspectives.
